messages.author: 8d7e6559e413a92b
messages.subject: Simulating autocorrelated errors
parts:
Hi All, 

My question is not technically specific to INLA; however, I suspect that this community will be best able to offer advice, so I hope you can forgive this being slightly off topic. 

All I want to do is simulate data for a BYM model, which means I need to simulate autocorrelated errors for an arbitrary lattice structure. These simulations will be part of a paper and that paper will be accompanied by a dashboard that will allow users to generate and sample from data with a specified degree of autocorrelation. Accordingly, I would like a method for simulating autocorrelation that relies on an intuitive parameters (e.g. rho). 

So far, I have experimented with a method I came across in the r-inla CAR documentation (http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/doc/latent/besagproper.pdf). Given INLAs CAR parameterization, that approach makes perfect sense. However, I would prefer to be able to explain the simulation without having to rely on explaining parameterization, too. 

I have also experimented with spdep's functions (InvIrM) for generating SAR random variables. I thought that would be an ideal approach, for my purposes, as it would allow me to focus on rho (an intuitive concept) and explain the linear algebra in supplemental materials. However, I am having trouble making spdep's functions work for me (probably due to my less than sophisticated understanding of linear algebra). 

Finally, I have come across no examples of simulating data for a BYM model with IVs, but examples must exist. 

Can anyone offer any advice regarding how I should simulate spatial autocorrelation, given the preference that the method is intuitively parameterized? Even just a paper that explains the methods that I describe above would be a great start. 

Thanks for your time!

Best,
Joe

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Simulating autocorrelated errors
parts:
Hi,
Brief answer: there are two separate issues: which specific parameterisation to use, and how to simulate from the resulting model. For the simulation part, you will need to construct the precision matrix (easy if you have the graph as an adjacency matrix, and use the standard cholesky method to sample (or just call inla.qsample() if you can use the inla package).

See http://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~flindgre/tmp/gmrf.pdf for details on the computational methods (it doesn’t discuss the necessary graph reordering details though; in inla, they are accessible through inla.qreoreding ) for sampling and conditioning.  The Rue and Held 2005 book on GMRFs is a good source for understanding GMRFs.

Finn
